Detractor

/dih-TRAK-ter/ — stress on TRAK · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A detractor is a person who belittles or runs down someone or something — often publicly, and again and again.

The architect's detractors called the new library an eyesore before the paint had even dried.

Worked Example

A young mayor launches a bike-lane program. One columnist devotes article after article to mocking the plan, sneering at her inexperience, and predicting the city will regret electing her.

The columnist is not weighing strengths and weaknesses — he is working, publicly and repeatedly, to pull the mayor's reputation down. A person doing that is her detractor. Because the criticism is ongoing and aimed at belittling, detractor is more precise than the neutral word "critic."

How Detractor Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

critic

critic: anyone who judges — a critic can be harsh, fair, or even friendly

naysayer

naysayer: someone who habitually says no and predicts failure

disparager

disparager: someone who talks a person or idea down as worthless

Antonyms

supporter

supporter: someone who backs a person or cause and defends it

admirer

admirer: someone who looks up to a person with warm approval

How Strong Is It? — observer → critic → naysayer → detractor

observer vs. detractor

observer vs. detractor: An observer merely watches and reports — no judgment at all, far from a detractor's steady attacks.

critic vs. detractor

critic vs. detractor: A critic judges — sometimes harshly, sometimes kindly. A detractor only ever pulls down.

naysayer vs. detractor

naysayer vs. detractor: A naysayer doubts and objects, but a detractor goes further: actively belittling, often in public and on repeat.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of detractor.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: down, away (Latin)

Root — tract

Root — tract: to draw, to pull (Latin trahere)

Suffix — -or

Suffix — -or: a person who does something

Put it together

Put it together: De (down) + tract (pull) + -or (a person who) — a detractor is literally 'one who pulls down.' Every public jab is another tug at someone's reputation. The pulling root is everywhere in English: a magnet attracts (pulls toward), a dentist extracts (pulls out), and a startled turtle retracts (pulls back) its head.

Use the root in a new word: extract

Use the root in a new word: extract: The dentist had to extract the cracked tooth, easing it out in one slow, careful pull.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / journalistic

Detractor is a favorite of news writing — "the mayor's detractors," "the plan's detractors" — and it usually travels with a possessive. Use it when the criticism is public, repeated, and aimed at pulling someone down; for a single fair judgment, the plain word "critic" is the better choice.
